correctness.rationale: Both source files reconstruct the 40-vertex cubic graph and shortest-path distances independently. One enumerates all 91,390 four-sets and 658,008 five-sets by uniqueness of distance tuples, retaining exactly 41,040 bases; the other uses independently computed 780-pair separation bitmasks to reproduce all counts. All 175 potential single swaps from every basis are checked, producing 670,930 undirected edges with reciprocal adjacency. The natural 40-element dihedral group is proved to preserve G, so eccentricity is constant on each of its 1,032 orbits. Full BFS from every orbit representative visits all 41,040 bases and yields radius 6, diameter 7 and exact eccentricity classes. The second program independently verifies connectivity and explicit witnesses; no unsupported inference from samples is used.

originality.rationale: The complete finite basis count, adjacency graph, and eccentricities are not implied by the known value of the metric dimension. The closely relevant 2014 and 2018 published treatments of GP(n,3), and a 2025 treatment for sufficiently large n, were inspected in their accessible substantive sections/full HTML; those sources study dimension bounds and exact dimension, not this optimal-state exchange graph. Searches of mathematical record summaries and primary publications found no statement covering all or part of these exact exchange metrics. The possibility of unpublished or unindexed exact counts, and uninspected pages of the 2014 PDF, remains a genuine priority risk, not a reason to claim global uniqueness.

value.rationale: The fixed graph GP(20,3) is a naturally exceptional case singled out by the published metric-dimension-five theorem. Exact counts and optimal-state reconfiguration quantify whether minimum five-landmark sensor layouts can be moved through other minimum layouts, the sharp maximum number of one-landmark replacements, and the structure/size of the exceptional peripheral configurations. This is a complete, motivated finite classification not implied by the known dimension or a generic textbook inequality. It makes no unsupported claim about the infinite Petersen family.
